en: The Essential Treatise on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
spoken by the Śramaṇa Seng Zhikě:
This Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom is truly the bright lamp for the great night of sentient beings and [the teaching] of all Buddhas.
"Life of Wisdom" (慧命): In Sanskrit, *prajñā* is translated as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*), and *pāramitā* is translated as "reaching the other shore" (*dào bī'àn*).

This means that one who possesses wisdom illuminates and shatters the afflictions (*kleśa*), does not succumb to the waves of birth and death, and transcends to wondrously accord with the fundamental source;
this is what is meant by "ascending to the other shore. The mind is thus likened to this sutra, for although a person has but a single body...
The hundred skeletal members and five viscera have the mind as their sovereign; though this scriptural text is concise, it is in truth the essence of six hundred fascicles of magnificent writing.
"Sūtra" (Jing) means that which is unchanging and constant throughout antiquity and the present, a direct path upon which those who encounter it may advance.
As for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, it is said that this Bodhisattva, by means of the aforementioned wisdom, perfectly illuminates emptiness and attains realization.

Regarding "Unobstructed," Master Zhao said: "If illumination does not lose its emptiness, one engages with existence without being burdened; if emptiness does not lose its illumination, one contemplates the void without becoming intoxicated.
By thus embracing both existence and non-existence while remaining detached from form and emptiness, one is able to both exist and not exist, and to both be empty and have form;
therefore, it is called 'sovereign mastery' (*svatantra*). As for sentient beings who cling to duality, even the followers of the Two Vehicles still possess partialities."
If one’s vision cannot achieve perfect penetration, one will not attain mastery. Wisdom and cleverness are vastly different from one another:
cleverness arises from external objects, whereas wisdom is born from the fundamental mind.
Therefore, while cleverness is subject to arising and ceasing, wisdom has no dependence; this is why it is non-arising and non-ceasing.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*" refers to the contemplative wisdom cultivated by this Bodhisattva, which differs from the partial and shallow [wisdom] of the Two Vehicles;

it is indeed the profound *prajñā*. Because it is the profound *prajñā*, it is able to illuminate thoroughly that form and emptiness are fundamentally non-dual and originally one true reality (*dharmatā*). It is simply that ordinary beings do not understand this, and thus they see form but do not see [emptiness].

The two vehicles of emptiness are biased attachments that perceive only emptiness while failing to see form—just as the fish and dragons in the waters of the Ganges regard it as their home, the devas regard it as lapis lazuli, the humans of the world regard it as flowing waves, and the hungry ghosts regard it as fierce flames;
what these four perceive is nothing more than their own mental projections. Only those who have awakened to the mind realize that there is no such thing as seeing form.

Since feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have likewise never been anything other than thus, it is said: "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When one clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, then all suffering and affliction are exhausted. Ordinary people are deluded and inverted; they do not awaken to this.
Because one clings to this body—a mere provisional combination of the four great elements—as being real, one rejoices upon hearing of its birth and grieves upon hearing of its death.

Yet one does not realize that when this body is examined through the lens of the four great elements, it is fundamentally unobtainable; who, then, is there to undergo birth and death? Since the body is thus, so too is this mind.
It is merely a shadow of false imagination and discursive clinging, composed of nothing more than the four aggregates (*skandhas*). If one examines these four aggregates...
Upon examining this mind, it too cannot be apprehended. Who then can be called a person afflicted by defilements?
One who does not realize this will feel joy upon hearing praise and sorrow and displeasure upon hearing blame; this is merely following one's whims and indulging one's consciousness.

If one does not transform consciousness into wisdom through contemplative practice, one will drift and sink into the ocean of suffering, tossed by waves thousands of fathoms high, emerging and submerging in a state of constant flux.

Changing heads and faces, feathers bristling horizontally and vertically—how could there ever be an end to this? Alas for sentient beings! Buddhahood is fundamentally already perfected, yet they refuse to accept it;
they seek it beyond their own nature, willingly taking up the burden themselves. Enduring such bitter poison, they still have not awakened.
Śāriputra was the preeminent disciple of the Buddha; his intelligence was peerless and his eloquence surpassed all others. The Buddha called him by name and addressed him, saying:
"The Bodhisattva, through wisdom, illuminates the five aggregates to their depths and forever parts from great suffering, taking a long farewell from the triple world.
Do you understand this? It is the emptiness within form, yet it does not abandon engagement with the world."
Regarding these "all dharmas having the characteristic of emptiness," this characteristic of emptiness refers to the illumination and vision of the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

This emptiness is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, fundamentally without defilement or purity, and fundamentally without increase or decrease. To explain this by means of the stages prior to the Path (*mārga-pūrva*), during the Path (*mārga-madhya*), and after the Path (*mārga-paścāt*) is not necessarily the case.
Why? Because when a practitioner illuminates the five aggregates with wisdom, form (*rūpa*) is cut off at once as empty. Thus, ordinary beings... [are severed].
When the Sage’s resolve is fully realized, his precious sword stands facing the sun; even a Buddha could not withstand its edge, let alone a bodhisattva or an ordinary person.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and no form.
"Regarding 'no realm of sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena, and so forth up to no realm of consciousness':

this means that by means of this wisdom, the Bodhisattva not only illuminates the emptiness of the five aggregates, but reaches the point where the twelve bases and eighteen realms are all likewise empty.
Why is it said that the five aggregates are the twelve bases, and the twelve bases are the eighteen realms? The Buddha [said].
Because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, the teachings are established according to their individual needs.

For those who are deluded regarding the mind but not regarding form, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are taught. For those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding the mind, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are taught.

For those who are deluded regarding both mind and form, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are taught. To state it briefly, these three—aggregates, bases, and elements—do not transcend form and mind.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.

There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom, nor is there one who attains. This means that when a bodhisattva illuminates this with wisdom, within this true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not only are the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) fundamentally empty, but even the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in their cyclic flow are empty. It is not merely that... [the text here indicates a negation of further elaboration].
It is only that saṃsāra is empty, yet cessation is also empty; it is not only cessation that is empty, for suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are all empty.

Not only are the various phenomena empty, but even this very wisdom that realizes emptiness—comprising the aggregates, bases, and elements, up to the wisdom of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—is unattainable. This is because when the object does not exist, the subject cannot stand alone. 10.

Although there are differences in the proficiency or lack thereof between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas regarding the two factors and the Four Noble Truths, to speak in summary, within true emptiness (śūnyatā) such distinctions do not exist.
Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, his mind is without hindrance; because he is without hindrance...
There is no fear; far removed from all inverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This means that this sutra is not only the fundamental principle for sentient beings to cross the stream of birth and death and ascend to the other shore, but it is likewise the very basis for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The stages of partial realization and ultimate perfection must also fundamentally derive from this.

This is surely intended as an exhortation to circulate this sutra, so that all sentient beings may rely upon Prajñā in their cultivation and progress, lest they be deluded and confused by Māras or heterodox teachers. Yongjia said:
"The Great Man wields the sword of wisdom; the edge of Prajñā is like the flaming vajra. It does not merely empty the hearts of externalists, but..."
Those who have once fallen away from the resolve to transcend the world— even those with such great courage as to daunt the celestial Māras, such ambition for liberation, such a power,
such a vision of the winds and clouds, and such an ardent disposition— should be able to reduce all things to ashes and smoke in an instant,
like a great mass of fire that consumes everything it touches. Otherwise, upon encountering even a slight object of desire, they will give rise to the sentiments of children.

Some have said that the Master’s commentary on this sutra does not distinguish between cause and effect nor arrange it into formal sections, appearing somewhat muddled and inconsistent with ancient conventions;

they feared it might be unsuitable. I replied to them: "The myriad sutras and treatises spoken by our Buddha across the five periods of teaching are no more than means to refine away the defilements of sentient beings' emotions and to cleanse their perspectives; if one's emotions..."
When the dust is cleared and the ground is seen to be level, it is truly a case of being in accord within what appears to be discord with ancient regulations;
why do you speak so much?
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, and an unsurpassed mantra.
This peerless mantra is able to eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. This is merely a praise of the efficacy and solemnity of Prajñā.
As for the spirit, it is subtle and wondrous among the myriad things, yet cannot be measured; if it could be measured, it would not be spiritual.
As for clarity, it responds perfectly to all phenomena without leaving a trace; if there were a trace, it would not be clear. That which is unsurpassed has nothing superior to it.

As for those above, if there were anyone superior to them, they would not occupy the highest position; being "unequaled" (asama-sama) means there is no one with whom they can be equaled, for their perfection and fullness are unsurpassed.
Guifeng said: "Pervasive and pure, within it nothing else can be contained—whom could it equal?
All of the above constitutes the explicit teaching of Prajñā. Furthermore, there are three aspects of Prajñā, namely: the letter (vyañjana),...

"Contemplating characters" means contemplating the true reality (*dharmatā*). Indeed, without characters there is no way to initiate contemplation; without contemplation there is no way to mirror the true reality.
Without the true reality, the Bodhisattva would have nothing toward which to aspire. What is this "aspiration"? It refers to realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). Now, realization has degrees of depth:
the shallow involves severing the views and afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the *rajas* (dust-like) delusions; the deep involves the complete uprooting of the fundamental source.
Fundamental ignorance is directly confronted until one reaches wondrous enlightenment;

although the three contemplations are cultivated simultaneously within a single mind, the power of the contemplation of emptiness predominates in severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the power of the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*) predominates in severing the ignorance of the sands of phenomena (*rajas*), and the power of the contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama*) takes the lead in severing fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Now, when the ground of insight is clear...
What difference is there between one who practices contemplation and one who possesses a field but does not plow it? Although they practice contemplation, their vision of the ground is not clear;
they are like a blind person walking on a path—not only unable to return home, I fear they will fall into pits and ravines.
If a person fears birth and death and loathes afflictions, nothing is better than contemplating the body through the four great elements and the four aggregates.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the principle of contemplating the body through the four great elements and contemplating the mind through the four aggregates is the Tathāgata’s way of cutting open his heart and gouging out his gallbladder—a skillful means intended to lead sentient beings, right upon this stinking physical shell and within these攀緣 (pán-yuán) shadows of perception, to attain immediate and wondrous awakening to the fact that this body and this mind are originally one true reality (*dharmatā*).
Yet, sentient beings continue to drift through birth and death, revolving in the cycle of saṃsāra.
The miserable realms are truly not obstructed by sounds, forms, wealth, profit, food, drink, men, or women;

rather, it is because one cannot view the body through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and view the mind through the four aggregates (*skandha*). If one perceives that there is a body to be obtained and a mind to be obstructed—when a body can be obtained, birth and death are manifest;
when a mind can be obstructed, hatred and attachment blaze forth—and thus birth and death become thick.
When hatred and attachment are deep, the primordial wisdom and radiance are buried; are Buddhas and sentient beings then two separate things?
A Buddha is nothing more than a person who is free from birth and death, and free from hatred and attachment. Sentient beings, however, possess birth and death, and possess hatred and attachment.
Regarding the Buddha’s contemplation of the body as the four elements: when a practitioner walks, stands, sits, or lies down, they should always maintain purity and mindfulness.

For the first time, observe this body: its skin, flesh, sinews, and bones fundamentally belong to the element of earth; its blood, vessels, mucus, saliva, and fluids fundamentally belong to the element of water;
its warmth belongs to fire; and its movement belongs to wind. When you examine it with discerning scrutiny, what "self" is there?
Yet now you grasp at it perversely and refuse to let go, recognizing it as real—how is this any different from two ghosts fighting over a stinking corpse? It is exactly like that.

This contemplation must be practiced for a long time; as it deepens, it gradually matures, and as it matures, it gradually gives rise to further cultivation until it reaches the point of complete refinement.

One must not neglect even the single character "refinement" (*lian*). If one is not truly a person who has resolved the matter of birth and death, then when confronted with favorable or adverse circumstances, one will be unable to shoulder the burden.
As for the contemplation of the mind within the four aggregates: first, one contemplates the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), investigating from where it arises, and tracing it back.
If one investigates this to its limit: does it arise suddenly without cause, or does it arise dependent upon objects?
If it could arise without cause, then while the preceding object has not yet been perceived and the fundamental mind is tranquil and lucid, how could there be what is called "delusory thought"?

If it arises dependent upon objects, then as the preceding objects shift and change, the mind also shifts and changes; how could this shifting and changing mind be my true self? If it were my true self...

The mind establishes heaven and earth, and all things take it as their root. If it were subject to change and transformation, how could it serve as the root of heaven and earth or the foundation of all things?
Therefore, know that change and transformation are merely shadows clung to through conditioned attachment.
As for the true mind, though dust arises, it is not born; though dust perishes, it does not perish. It illuminates objects without being burdened by them. Thus...
Vipaśyin Buddha spoke in verse: "Borrowing the four great elements to constitute body and mind, The mind is fundamentally without birth;
it exists because of objects. If the external objects do not exist, the mind likewise does not exist. Sin and merit are like illusions—arising and then ceasing.

This verse is the World-Honored One’s great compassionate presentation of the essential framework of dependent origination and non-arising. If one can awaken to this, the wondrous essence of the Heart Sūtra is fully realized.

This is what is meant by "dependent origination is non-arising": it means that the mind does not arise of itself; arising must be through objects. Objects do not manifest of themselves; manifestation must be through the mind.
That the mind does not arise of itself is because the mind lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); that objects do not manifest of themselves is because objects lack intrinsic nature.

When both mind and objects lack intrinsic nature, non-arising is manifested before us; yet, when mind and objects are devoid of intrinsic nature, dependent origination is not abandoned. The mind remains.

Since this is true for a single mote of dust, it is so for all phenomena. This principle is called the *dharmadhātu* in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (real aspect) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Some may say: "This scripture takes the deconstruction of characteristics as its primary tenet and the discourse on emptiness as its ultimate aim;
how could it possibly share the same track as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Now, both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* manifest the Perfect [Teaching].

I take this sutra as my fundamental principle; its esoteric discourse on the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) represents the established pronouncements of the ancients, and is not the result of my own presumptuous or forced interpretations.
Alas! Sentient beings fail to comprehend this meaning due to their doubts: within that which is bodiless, they falsely perceive a body; within that which is mindless, they falsely perceive a mind.
They do not realize that the form of the bodiless body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and that the state of the mindless mind...
The Mind Illuminating All Beings: Is this body and mind not indeed lofty, profound, and mysterious?

Yet, within our daily lives, at every moment we respond to conditions, it has never failed to be vividly manifest. As the Old Man of Donghua said regarding the *Avataṃsaka*: "The Buddha-dharma is in the midst of daily life;
it is in the places of putting on clothes and eating meals, in the places of defecating and urinating, and in the lifting of the mind and the movement of thought."
"That is not yet it," said Layman Pang. "In daily life there is no distinction; it is only that I alone find harmony.
Spiritual powers and wondrous functions are used in carrying water and hauling firewood. Now, regarding this principle, there are those who have attained awakening but have not yet practiced;

those who have practiced but have not yet perfected it; and those who have realized it and are enjoying its fruition. Suppose there were someone here who, having attained a slight awakening, [is asked]:
If one does not practice yet claims to have already realized it, then cultivation and realization will be cast aside;
such folly will lead to a state of utter embarrassment on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. This humble writer does not venture to join the ranks of those who debate doctrinal tenets.

However, as the Layman Haiyang happened to inquire about this matter, I could not help but compose this spontaneously according to my own thoughts. Therefore, I do not request the Three Jewels to bear witness to it.
This is the verse for the bestowal of empowerment.
"Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā" is the esoteric teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
Since it is called "esoteric," I, your humble servant, dare not venture to discuss it further.
Essential Treatise on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Concluded)
